growth_story.headline: Serbia's income per person grew fast to 2008, nearly stalled after the global crisis, then sped up again to 4.3 percent a year from 2017.
growth_story.arc: Serbia's income per person grew 5.2 percent a year over 1996–2008, with one sharp fall of 10.0 percent in 1999; the IMF links the strong years of the 2000s to quick stabilization, opening up and privatization after a decade of sanctions. Over 2009–2016 growth fell to 0.6 percent a year, as the global financial crisis, the European debt crisis and Serbia's own large imbalances kept income per person almost flat. The IMF credits careful economic policy and broad reforms begun in 2014 for what followed: growth of 4.3 percent a year over 2017–2025, and an average of 4.3 percent over the last decade against 2.0 percent in 2006–2015, with income per person at its highest level yet in 2025. Foreign direct investment, much more public investment, more people in work and faster productivity growth all fed this era, even as the population shrank. Growth slowed to 2.6 percent in 2025 amid domestic protests and sanctions on the main oil company, and the World Bank reports a mild recovery in 2026.

threads.title: Opening up after sanctions
threads.text: After a decade of sanctions and turmoil in the 1990s, Serbia steadied its economy, opened trade and banking, and sold state firms after 2000. The IMF calls the years before the global crisis a golden period of strong productivity gains, though it says reform effort stalled from the late 2000s.

threads.title: Crisis and imbalances, 2008–2015
threads.text: The global financial crisis hit an economy that already had large imbalances, and the European debt crisis that followed deepened the blow. Income per person barely moved between 2009 and 2016.

citations.title: Navigating Serbia's Economic Future: The Crucial Role of Productivity (Selected Issues Paper SIP/2025/111)

threads.title: Foreign capital and investment
threads.text: From the mid-2010s both private and public investment rose, with private investment helped by large inflows of foreign direct investment. The World Bank reports that foreign direct investment stayed weak in the first half of 2026.

citations.title: Navigating Serbia's Economic Future: The Crucial Role of Productivity (Selected Issues Paper SIP/2025/111)
citations.quote: private investment almost doubled in 2023 compared to its level in 2014, also helped by strong foreign direct investment (FDI) inflows

citations.title: Macro Poverty Outlook: Serbia (October 2026)

threads.title: A shrinking, emigrating population
threads.text: Serbia's population is falling and people are leaving, yet more of those who stay have found work, so jobs still added to growth in the last decade. The IMF projects that, without reforms, labor will add less to growth in the years ahead because of the population trend.

citations.title: Navigating Serbia's Economic Future: The Crucial Role of Productivity (Selected Issues Paper SIP/2025/111)
citations.quote: enabling labor to contribute 1 percentage point to growth over 2016–24, despite a shrinking population and net emigration

citations.title: Navigating Serbia's Economic Future: The Crucial Role of Productivity (Selected Issues Paper SIP/2025/111)
citations.quote: Absent reforms, labor is projected to contribute only 0.5 percent to growth in the medium term given unfavorable demographics.

threads.title: Protests and oil company sanctions
threads.text: In 2025 domestic protests and sanctions on NIS, the country's main oil company, slowed growth and raised energy risks. In May 2026 IMF staff still listed delays in settling the NIS case among the risks to growth.

since_last_year.text: Growth in income per person slowed to 2.6 percent in 2025, as domestic protests and sanctions on the oil company NIS weighed on the economy. In 2026 the World Bank reports a mild recovery as the oil refinery and the Stellantis car plant started up again and car exports grew. In May 2026 IMF staff named a wider conflict in the Middle East, and the energy market disruption it brings, as a new risk to growth.

growth_story.tension: The World Bank describes Serbia's total output growth since 2022 as solid. Income per person grew faster than that, by 5.3, 4.4 and 4.5 percent in 2022–2024, because the population is shrinking and people are emigrating. Part of the recent rise in income per person therefore reflects fewer people, not only more output.
